prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned Romanian prose that builds from memory, the body and dream an encyclopedic inner cosmos, a sustained imaginative project of the large-scale novel.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: Mircea Cărtărescu as sole laureate. The exchange did not weaken the case on the common criteria, but it sharpened what the case has to rest on. His voice is distinctive. Public knowledge of Blinding (the Orbitor sequence) and Solenoid points to long, nested architectures, recurring image systems, and memory, the body and dream treated as one metaphysical subject. That is a formal achievement and not only a thematic one. Intellectual and imaginative depth lies in how the work turns private consciousness into a cosmology. The oeuvre looks consolidated, with Solenoid generally seen as a late major work, so premature judgment is not my concern. On the chair's scope question I now favor anchoring the citation on the prose, as I did in round 1, with poetry understood as an origin and not named as an independently assessed pillar. That follows Carlberg's position and Mattson's point that poetry-as-base is a hypothesis. The citation should not claim more than we can weigh. This is a literary judgment from general public knowledge, not from independently verified reading, and the unanimous opening is not merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and unresolved. I judge dense, rhythmic Romanian prose only through translation, and the long digressive forms may read as depth to some readers and as accumulation to others. My own test from round 1, whether later volumes deepen their image systems or recirculate them, is still not settled by anything in this exchange. As publicly described, Solenoid has a different narrative frame from the Orbitor sequence, which suggests some variation. I cannot confirm from that alone that it amounts to development. If Romanian-language criticism or a reader of the originals showed that the late volumes mainly restate the earlier ones, my confidence in sustained quality across the whole body of work would drop. Thin translated coverage of the poetry and early work also means the oeuvre is less visible to me than its peaks.

responses.point: Carlberg would anchor a Cărtărescu citation on the novels, with poetry as an origin of the vision and not an independently assessed pillar, because translation coverage of the poetry is thin. She also says a Carson citation would have to separate original work from scholarship and translation.
responses.response: I agree on the citation basis and have kept my wording prose-anchored. Naming poetry as a pillar would assert something none of us can weigh. On Carson I agree the scope can be stated, around formal reinvention in the original poetry, verse narrative and essays. It is harder to state and test than Cărtărescu's, because part of the force of the book-objects depends on physical design that a citation cannot capture. I keep Carson as my first alternative because the voice and invention are real. A defined citation would not by itself answer whether many short or fragmentary books carry whole-oeuvre weight.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg names prose and poetry jointly in his citation and argues the books are built, not merely long. He ranked Can Xue eighth because he cannot tell whether four decades of consistent method is deepening or restatement.
responses.response: I take the argument that the books are built, and it is why I read the length as potential architecture. I still would not name poetry jointly, for the evidentiary reason Carlberg and Mattson give. On Can Xue I share your uncertainty but not your conclusion. Without a firm view of variation across a partial translated corpus, I cannot treat consistency as a defect, and I cannot treat it as a merit either. That keeps her at fifth for me, below the candidates whose trajectory I can follow more confidently, and not out of contention.

responses.point: Sward says that if the committee valued formal reinvention of a language or genre over expansion of an established visionary mode, Tawada or Adonis would have a stronger claim than Cărtărescu. She does not hold this as her preference.
responses.response: That is the most useful challenge to my own weighting, because it concerns what the criteria reward and not only evidence. I find Cărtărescu's work more than an extension of a visionary tradition, since its scale and patterning are themselves a formal invention. I accept that this is arguable. Adonis is the stronger of the two cases for me, with seven decades of work and documented renewal of Arabic poetic language, and the public political commentary must stay out of it. But I cannot assess the achievement in Arabic prosody, which is why he stays an alternative. I did not rank Tawada in my top eight and cannot compare her without competence in both Japanese and German, so I do not move her.

responses.point: Mattson says the claim that poetry is the base of the prose project is the part of the case she can least verify, and that it should be treated as a hypothesis. She also doubts that Carson's cumulative weight exceeds Cărtărescu's, since much of it is short or fragmentary.
responses.response: I accept the hypothesis framing, and it has changed my wording. The citation names only what the prose supports. I also share your weighing of Carson. Autobiography of Red and Nox show real force and invention, but sustained major-form achievement is harder to establish for her than for a novelist with a large sequence. I would add that this is a difference in how easily the case can be tested, not a verdict that Carson is lesser. It is why she is an alternative for me and not my preference.

responses.point: Olsson says durability across the longest works cannot be settled from public reputation alone, and that a citation should rest on the imaginative project and not on any single volume. He accepts that this uncertainty remains real.
responses.response: I agree, and I would state it more strongly in my own case. My conviction is conditional on the late volumes deepening the earlier image systems, and I cannot show that from translation. I still prefer the citation to name the whole project and not one title, for the reason you give. On the chair's question about P000, I do not regard no award as preferable. The shared reservations are limits of access and not findings against the work, and I would want that distinction recorded.

uncertainties: Whether the late long novels deepen the earlier image systems or mainly repeat them cannot be settled from my public knowledge or from translation.
How much of the density, rhythm and musicality of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose survives translation.
Translation coverage of his poetry and early work is thin, so a unified oeuvre across genres is partly inferred, and the citation therefore anchors on prose.
Adonis and Tawada depend on Arabic prosody and on Japanese and German corpora that I cannot assess directly. Can Xue's partial translated corpus prevents a firm view of variation across decades.
How the committee should weigh hybrid and object-based work (Carson) and a compact oeuvre (Michon) under 'significance across the writer's body of work' is unresolved.
I have not independently verified any source or read the works for this exercise. Carlberg's simulated vote is a modeling assumption, and the full Academy's decision is not simulated.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. No recusal-relevant connection to any shortlisted writer is apparent from the supplied profile. Documented connections are to Selma Lagerlöf as a biographical subject, to collaborator Kate Larson, to David Håkansson, who was elected with me, and to committee colleagues. My own practice, with its parallel narratives, myths and fairy tales, is context and not evidence of a preference for any candidate. This disclosure is not adjudicated.
